content.text:
The original `0.svg` was a single empty root element with no drawing in it, so there was no artwork to refine. I rewrote it as a well-formed blank canvas with sensible defaults. The file now reads:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="100" height="100" viewBox="0 0 100 100" role="img" aria-labelledby="svg0-title">
  <title id="svg0-title">Untitled graphic</title>
</svg>
```

What changed:

- **XML declaration** with UTF-8 encoding, the convention for standalone SVG files on disk.
- **Explicit dimensions** and a matching `viewBox`, so every renderer agrees on the intrinsic size and the graphic scales cleanly. Without them, browsers and command-line tools each fall back to different default sizes.
- **Accessible name** through an image role and a title element linked by `aria-labelledby`, so assistive technology announces the graphic instead of skipping it or reading nothing.

Verification was partly blocked. The sandbox denied both `xmllint` and a Python XML parse, and this session has no way to approve prompts, so I could not run an automated well-formedness check or a test render. The `file` tool still identifies the result as an SVG image, and I checked the markup by inspection: three elements, matching close tags, quoted attributes.

Two things to know. The canvas size is a placeholder I chose and is easy to change in the three numeric attributes:

Canvas size: 100 × 100 user units

The file still draws nothing, because the original drew nothing. To add actual content, I need to know what the graphic should depict.
